01.note: Rabbi Yehoshua had disagreed with Rabban Gamliel, the head of the court, over which day was Yom Kippur. Ordered to appear on the day his own reckoning made Yom Kippur, he came carrying his staff and his money. When Rabban Gamliel saw him, he rose from his chair, kissed him on the head, and greeted him as 'my teacher and my student': teacher because he had taught Torah in public, student because he obeyed Rabban Gamliel's decree. He added: fortunate is the generation in which the greater heed the lesser.
01.why: The Gemara has just taught that whoever is appointed leader of his generation must be obeyed like the greatest of the great. Rabbi Yehoshua, the greater scholar, submitting to Rabban Gamliel's ruling is that teaching in action.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who disputed Rabban Gamliel's calendar; Rabban Gamliel calls him his teacher, since he taught Torah in public.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head of the court, who ordered Rabbi Yehoshua to appear and then received him with honor.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
An argument from the stronger case to the weaker: if something holds in a less likely case, it surely holds in a more likely one.
The Day of Atonement, a fast day on which carrying a staff and money is forbidden. Coming with them on that date meant treating it as an ordinary weekday.

02.note: The Sage Levi came to a certain place, and a man complained to him: 'So-and-so keva'a from me.' Levi did not know the word, so he went and asked in the study hall, where he was told it means 'robbed', as in the verse 'Will a man rob God?' Later, Rava from Barnish told Rav Ashi that had he been there, he would simply have asked the man how, with what and why he was keva'a, and worked out the meaning himself. The Gemara explains that Levi thought the man was raising a question of prohibition, where such questions would not have helped.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting cases in which the Sages learned the meaning of a rare word in Scripture from how ordinary people spoke in particular places. This one explains the verb in Malachi 3:8.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who visited a certain place and could not understand a man's complaint.

people.name: Rava from Barnish
people.about: A Sage who said how he would have worked out the word's meaning had he been in Levi's place.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage to whom Rava from Barnish made his remark.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages gathered to learn and discuss Torah, and where a question like Levi's could be put to other scholars.

03.note: The Sages did not know what the word seirugin meant. One day they heard the maidservant in the house of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi call out to Sages who were coming into the house in small groups, one after another: 'How long will you come in seirugin seirugin?' From this they understood that the word means 'at intervals'.
03.why: This is one of a run of anecdotes in which the meaning of a puzzling word in the Mishna or Scripture is learned from everyday speech, here from the household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in the household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whose everyday speech taught the Sages several rare words.

terms.meaning: Used alone, the title refers to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sage who compiled the Mishna.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

04.note: The Sages did not know what the word haloglogot meant, though it appears in several early teachings. One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house speak to a man she saw scattering his purslane plants: 'How long will you scatter your haloglogot?' So they learned that haloglogot means purslane.
04.why: Another in the Gemara's string of cases where an obscure word was explained by overhearing the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household whose speech revealed the meaning of the word.

terms.meaning: A leafy plant, eaten as a vegetable, that grows low and spreads along the ground.
Teachings of the early Sages: those collected in the Mishna (mishnayot) and those left out of it (baraitot).

05.note: The Sages did not know what salseleha meant in the verse 'Salseleha and it will exalt you,' which speaks of wisdom. One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house say to a man who was curling his hair: 'How long will you mesalsel your hair?' From this they understood the verse to mean: turn wisdom over and over, and it will exalt you.
05.why: Part of the Gemara's series of words in Scripture whose meaning the Sages learned from the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household whose words explained the verse.

06.note: The Sages did not know the meaning of the words in Isaiah's verse 'And I will sweep it with the broom of destruction.' One day they heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house tell a fellow worker: 'Take a broom and sweep the house,' using the same words, and so they understood the verse.
06.why: Another in the Gemara's run of puzzling words in Scripture explained by overhearing the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi's house
people.about: A servant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household; her instruction to a fellow worker explained the verse.

07.note: The Sages did not know what yehavkha meant in the verse 'Cast your yehavkha upon the Lord and He will sustain you.' Rabba bar bar Hana told how he was once traveling with an Arab while carrying a load, and the Arab said to him: 'Take your yehav and throw it on my camel.' From this he learned that yehav means a load.
07.why: The last of the Gemara's series of rare words explained from everyday speech; this time the source is not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's maidservant but an Arab traveler.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who learned the meaning of the word from a traveling companion.

people.name: the Arab
people.about: A traveler with a camel who offered to carry Rabba bar bar Hana's load.

08.note: Once Rosh Hashana fell on Shabbat, and people from all the towns gathered in Yavne. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai said to the sons of Beteira: 'Let us sound the shofar.' They answered: 'Let us discuss it.' He told them: 'Let us sound it, and discuss it afterward.' Once the shofar had been sounded, they said: 'Now let us discuss it.' He replied: 'The horn has already been heard in Yavne, and one does not argue against a ruling after it has been acted on.'
08.why: The Gemara has just explained that the Sages forbade sounding the shofar on Shabbat, lest someone carry it in public. The mishna says that after the Temple's destruction Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai allowed it in Yavne; this account shows how that happened.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who led the gathering at Yavne and had the shofar sounded on Shabbat.

people.name: the sons of Beteira
people.about: Leading legal authorities, who wanted to debate the question before the shofar was sounded.

terms.meaning: A ram's horn blown on Rosh Hashana, the Jewish New Year.
A town where the Sages' court sat after the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

09.note: A woman was summoned to a lawsuit before Ameimar in Neharde'a. Ameimar then went to Mehoza for a time, and she did not follow him there, so he wrote a document of excommunication against her. Rav Ashi challenged him: the mishna says that witnesses go only to the court's usual meeting place, even if its head is elsewhere. Ameimar answered that this applies only to witnesses who report the new moon, who must not be discouraged from coming in future. In money cases, he said, 'the borrower is servant to the lender'.
09.why: The mishna has just stated Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's rule that witnesses must go to the court's meeting place rather than follow its head. The Gemara uses this case to show the rule is limited to testimony about the new moon.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a who excommunicated a woman for not following him to Mehoza.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who challenged Ameimar's ruling by citing the mishna.

terms.meaning: A court order that put a person under a ban, cutting them off from the community, until they obeyed the court.
The court began each month on the word of witnesses who had seen the new moon, so it needed them to keep coming.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

10.note: Rabbi Eliezer had a vineyard in its fourth year east of Lod, beside the village of Tavi, and he wanted to declare its fruit ownerless for the poor. His students told him: 'Our teacher, your colleagues have already voted on this and permitted it.' The Gemara explains that 'your colleagues' means Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.
10.why: Rav Pappa holds that one of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's nine ordinances concerned fourth-year fruit grown near Jerusalem, which had to be carried there to fill its markets. This account is his evidence that the requirement was cancelled.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Owner of a fourth-year vineyard near Lod, who wanted to give its fruit to the poor.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer's students
people.about: They told him his colleagues had already voted to permit the fruit.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Gemara says he is the 'colleagues' the students meant.

terms.meaning: Fruit from a vine's fourth year is holy and must be eaten in Jerusalem, or redeemed for money. Vines within a day's walk of Jerusalem had to bring the fruit itself.
Property given up by its owner so that anyone, here the poor, may take it.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

11.note: When the court fixed the year's calendar in Usha, Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka led the Rosh Hashana prayer before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, following Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri's order of the blessings. Rabban Shimon told him: 'That was not the custom in Yavne.' On the second day Rabbi Hanina, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, led the prayer following Rabbi Akiva's order, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: 'This was the custom in Yavne.'
11.why: The Gemara is debating where in the Rosh Hashana prayer the blessings of Kingship and the holiness of the day belong. Afterward it asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel could approve Rabbi Akiva's order, when he places these blessings differently himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: Led the prayer at Usha in the order of Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri, and was told it was not the Yavne custom.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage before whom the prayer was led, who judged each leader against the custom of Yavne.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: Led the prayer on the second day in the order of Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: A Sage whose order of the Rosh Hashana blessings the first prayer leader followed.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage whose order of the blessings the second prayer leader followed.

terms.meaning: The court's act of fixing the calendar, deciding when months and the new year begin.
The leader of public prayer stood in front of the congregation, often at a lower place, so leading the prayer is called 'descending'.
One of the special blessings of the Rosh Hashana prayer, made up of verses that proclaim God as King.

12.note: Rabbi Abbahu was walking behind Rabbi Yohanan and reciting the Shema prayer. When he reached alleys that were filthy with excrement, where words of Torah may not be spoken, he fell silent. Once he had passed through, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could go on from where he had stopped. Rabbi Yohanan told him: if you paused long enough to have said the whole of it, go back to the beginning.
12.why: The Gemara has ruled that, for Rabbi Yohanan, shofar blasts heard at different times of day still count, and has said his stricter rule about long pauses is his teacher's view. This story challenges that, since Rabbi Yohanan seems to rule strictly himself.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage walking behind Rabbi Yohanan, who broke off his Shema in a filthy alley.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Abbahu was following, who told him to start the Shema again.

terms.meaning: The central declaration of Jewish faith, 'Hear O Israel', recited every morning and evening.

13.note: Reish Lakish was swimming in the Jordan River when Rabba bar bar Hana came and gave him a hand. Reish Lakish said to him: 'My God! I hate you,' meaning the Jews of Babylonia. He explained with a verse from the Song of Songs: had all of them come up to the Land of Israel together, like a wall, in the days of Ezra, they would have been like silver, which rot cannot touch. Because they came only partly, like doors, they are like cedar, which rot does attack.
13.why: The Gemara has been asking whether the generations of the First or the Second Temple were greater. Reish Lakish's outburst explains why the Second Temple fell short: not all the exiles returned. The Gemara then doubts he would have spoken with Rabba bar bar Hana at all.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel, swimming in the Jordan, who rebuked the Babylonian Jews.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who gave Reish Lakish a hand out of the river.

terms.meaning: The time when exiles came back from Babylonia to the Land of Israel and built the Second Temple; many stayed behind.
God's presence dwelling among the people, which the translation says was only partly felt in the Second Temple.

14.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of an examiner who was checking mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori, when a Roman official caught him and fined him a thousand zuz. The Gemara asks: did not Rabbi Elazar say that people on their way to do a commandment come to no harm? It answers that where the danger is constant, one may not rely on that, just as Samuel feared Saul would kill him, even when God sent him.
14.why: Abaye has explained that the gates of Mehoza had no mezuza because of the danger from the gentiles living there. Rabbi Yehuda's incident shows that checking public mezuzot really could bring trouble.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: the examiner
people.about: A man checking mezuzot in Tzippori's upper market, who was caught and fined.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who taught that those on a mission for a commandment come to no harm.

people.name: Samuel
people.about: The prophet sent by God to anoint David, who feared Saul would kill him.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll of Torah verses fixed to a doorpost, as the Torah commands. Public ones on city gates were checked from time to time.
A silver coin; a thousand zuz was a very large sum.

15.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori, who was appointed to serve in place of a High Priest who had become disqualified. When the High Priest could serve again, the Sages ruled that he returns to his service. Yosef ben Elem could serve neither as High Priest, because two equal High Priests would breed hatred, nor as an ordinary priest, because in holy matters one raises a person up and does not bring him down.
15.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree about a stand-in High Priest once the original returns. Rabbi Yosei cites this case to prove his view that the stand-in may serve in neither role, and the Gemara then rules like him.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as proof of his opinion.

people.name: Yosef ben Elem
people.about: A priest from Tzippori appointed to stand in for a disqualified High Priest.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who alone performed the Yom Kippur service and wore eight special garments; an ordinary priest wore four.
Something, such as ritual impurity, that temporarily prevented the High Priest from serving.

16.note: A Sadducee serving as High Priest on Yom Kippur prepared the incense outside and only then carried it into the Holy of Holies, as the Sadducees held it should be done. He came out overjoyed. His father met him and said: 'My son, though we are Sadducees, we fear the Pharisees.' The son answered that all his life he had been troubled by the verse 'For I will appear in the cloud above the Ark cover,' and now that he had the chance, how could he not fulfill it? The Sages said that within a few days he died, was thrown on a garbage heap, and worms came out of his nose. Others say an angel struck him in the face as he came out, and his fellow priests found the mark of a calf's hoof between his shoulders.
16.why: The mishna says the Elders made the High Priest swear not to change the service, and the Gemara has just explained the fear: that he would light the incense outside, as the Sadducees did. This story shows what happened when one did.

people.name: the Sadducee
people.about: A High Priest who followed the Sadducee practice with the incense on Yom Kippur.

people.name: his father
people.about: Also a Sadducee, who warned his son that they feared the Pharisees.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who taught the version in which an angel struck the High Priest.

terms.meaning: Rival groups in Second Temple times. The Pharisees followed the Sages' oral tradition; the Sadducees rejected it and read Scripture their own way.
The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, and only on Yom Kippur.
Fragrant spices burned on coals. On Yom Kippur the High Priest offered them in the Holy of Holies, where they made a cloud of smoke.
A collection of early teachings arranged like the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, filling in details it leaves out.

17.note: Rav came to Rabbi Sheila's town, where he was not known. Rabbi Sheila had no one to repeat his lecture aloud to the public, so Rav took the job, and explained the phrase keriat hagever as 'the call of the man'. Rabbi Sheila told him to say 'the call of the rooster'. Rav answered with a saying: a flute is music to noblemen but means nothing to weavers. When I said this before Rabbi Hiyya, he raised no objection, and you correct me? Rabbi Sheila realized who he was: 'Is the Master Rav? Let the Master rest.' Rav replied: 'If you hired yourself out to him, comb his wool.' Some say he answered that in holy matters one raises a person up and does not bring him down.
17.why: The mishna uses keriat hagever to mark a time in the Temple, and Rav and Rabbi Sheila disagree over its meaning. This story is their disagreement as it came up in a lecture; the Gemara then cites an early teaching for each side.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage, unknown in Rabbi Sheila's town, who volunteered to repeat Rabbi Sheila's lecture to the public.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: The town's leading scholar, who corrected Rav and then recognized him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage for whom Rav had once given the same explanation without objection.

terms.meaning: A speaker who stood beside a Sage giving a public lecture, repeating and explaining his words loudly to the audience.
A phrase from the mishna marking an early-morning time in the Temple. Gever can mean both 'man' and 'rooster'.

18.note: King Agrippa was traveling on the road and heard the voice of Gevini the Crier, the Temple official who woke the priests each morning, from three parasangs away. When the king got home, he sent him gifts. The Gemara adds that the High Priest's voice was greater still: once, when he called out 'Please, God' in his Yom Kippur confession, he was heard in Jericho, which Rabba bar bar Hana said, quoting Rabbi Yohanan, is ten parasangs from Jerusalem.
18.why: Rav explained the mishna's keriat hagever as 'the call of the man', and the Gemara has cited an early teaching about Gevini the Crier's call to support him. This incident shows how far that call carried.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king who heard the Crier's voice from far away and sent him gifts.

people.name: Gevini the Crier
people.about: A Temple official whose morning call to priests, Levites and Israelites carried three parasangs.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Quotes Rabbi Yohanan on the distance from Jerusalem to Jericho.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who said Jericho is ten parasangs from Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance; the translation puts three parasangs at slightly more than eight miles.
On Yom Kippur the High Priest laid his hands on his bull offering and confessed the sins of himself and his household aloud, calling on God's name.

19.note: Rav Huna read the verse 'Saul was one year old when he began to reign' as meaning that Saul was as free of sin as a one-year-old. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objected: why not say he was like a one-year-old smeared with mud and excrement? That night Rav Nahman was shown a frightening dream. He said: 'I humbly submit to you, bones of Saul son of Kish.' He was shown a frightening dream again, and this time said: 'I humbly submit to you, bones of Saul son of Kish, king of Israel.'
19.why: The Gemara is weighing the sins of Saul and David and how each was punished. Rav Nahman's dreams warn against belittling Saul, and the discussion goes on to ask why Saul's line did not keep the throne.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who mocked Rav Huna's reading of a verse about Saul and was then troubled by frightening dreams.

people.name: Saul son of Kish
people.about: The first king of Israel, whose bones Rav Nahman addressed in apology.

20.note: Two priests were running neck and neck up the ramp to the altar. One of them reached the last four cubits first, and the other took a knife and stabbed him in the heart. Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps of the Temple's entrance hall and cried: 'Hear, my brothers of the house of Israel!' He quoted the Torah's law of a slain man found in a field and asked who must bring the heifer whose neck is broken here, the city or the Temple courts. All the people burst into tears. The boy's father came and found him still convulsing. He said: 'May he be your atonement. My son is still convulsing, so the knife has not become impure.' The Tosefta comments that the purity of vessels mattered more to them than bloodshed.
20.why: The mishna tells of a priest whose leg was broken in this race, which led the Sages to replace it with a lottery. After this account the Gemara asks which incident came first and why the murder alone did not end the race.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who rose on the Temple steps and addressed the people after the stabbing.

people.name: the father of the boy
people.about: Father of the stabbed young priest, who worried that the knife not become impure.

terms.meaning: The sloped walkway up to the altar. Priests raced up it for the right to clear the ashes, and the first to reach within four cubits of the top won.
A rite in the Torah: when a murdered body is found and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest town break a young cow's neck to atone.
A state that bars a person or object from Temple use. A knife touching a dead body would become impure; while the boy lived, it would not.
A collection of early teachings arranged like the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, filling in details it leaves out.
